memberdef.name: set_reverse_edges

detaileddescription.para: the received edges, whose targets are home ids and whose sources are graph ids; computes remote_ids

Selects the home rows [begin, end) for the next join() and sets remote_ids to the remote ids of their neighborhoods that have a new member. set_reverse_edges() selects all home rows. join() calls on disjoint ranges that cover the home rows need only the remote ids of their range. With one distance per pair, they give the same rows as one join() on all rows. When a pair can get two distances (see above), a range can send a candidate to a remote row that one join() would cut, so the rows can differ slightly.

memberdef.name: join_impl

detaileddescription.para: whether the neighborhood of home row t has a new member, so that its local join computes distances
The remote ids of the home rows [begin, end), sorted. With the reverse lists: the remote ids of the neighborhoods that have a new member, which are the only ones that a local join reads.
The rows of one process in an NN-descent round over a graph that is split between processes (for example a distributed build, after the per-partition builds).

Graph ids are int64. Process p owns the ids owner_begin[p] .. owner_begin[p + 1] - 1 and holds their rows and vectors in that order. A round has four steps. Between the steps, the caller sends the lists to the other processes; each list is grouped by destination process, with one count per process.
reverse_edges(): the edges u -> v of the home rows, for the owner of v.
set_reverse_edges(): the received edges. Each home row keeps its R nearest reverse edges by (distance, source). The remote ids are the sorted ids that other processes own, of the neighborhoods that have a new member: a local join of a neighborhood without one computes no distances.
join(): with the vectors and the K-th distances of the remote ids, the local joins of the home rows, as in DeterministicNNDescent::round(). join() inserts the candidates for home rows and returns the candidates for remote rows, the K best for each row. With select_rows(), several join() calls can each cover a range of the home rows, with the remote ids of that range only.
insert_candidates(): the candidates that the other processes sent, in any order, then end_round(), which returns the number of home rows that changed. With the same rows, a round gives the same rows as DeterministicNNDescent::round() on the whole graph, except for the order of equal distances. The result does not depend on the thread count or on the order in which the lists arrive.

The candidates for a remote row can include ids that are already in the row: the owner drops them in insert_candidates(). A pair can get two distances that differ in the last bits: init() computes some distances directly and the local joins from the squared norms, and coded remote vectors differ from the home vectors. The cases below that give "the same rows" assume one value per pair; otherwise the rows can differ slightly, but are still the same in every run with the same input.
